sections.h: Leviathan in Job: God's creature, not his rival (Job 41)
sections.b: Job uses the old picture of the sea monster more than any other book: "those who are ready to wake Leviathan" (Job 3:8), "Am I the Sea, or am I the Dragon?" (Job 7:12), and God's crushing of Rahab (Job 9:13; 26:12–13). In the LORD's second speech the monster returns in full (Job 41:1–34): hooks and harpoons cannot take it, its scales are rows of shields, fire and smoke pour from its mouth, the gods are afraid when it rises, and "it is king of all the proud creatures" (Job 41:34). Yet God does not fight it. He describes it with pride, as something he made. Job 41:1–8 is numbered Job 40:25–32 in Hebrew Bibles, and Job 41:9–34 is Hebrew 41:1–26.

sections.h: Four ways to read Leviathan in Job
sections.b: A real animal. Since Samuel Bochart (1663) many have said the Nile crocodile, hunted with hooks and harpoons, whose eyes at dawn were the Egyptian sign for sunrise; older Christian writers (Aquinas, Calvin) said the whale. The chaos monster. At Ugarit, Baal struck down Lotan, "the fleeing serpent, the twisting serpent, the mighty one with seven heads" (KTU 1.5 i 1–3, paraphrased), and Isaiah 27:1 uses the same words: on that day the LORD with his hard, great and strong sword will punish Leviathan the fleeing serpent, Leviathan the twisting serpent, and will kill the dragon in the sea (a fresh rendering; Isaiah is not yet translated on this site). Fire-breathing and the fear of the gods (Job 41:18–25) suit the myth. Both. Many scholars (Keel, Habel, Newsom) think the poet drew a crocodile in mythic colors, making the chaos beast a creature. Evil itself. Christian readers from Gregory the Great on read Leviathan as the devil, the dragon of Revelation 12:9.

Jewish tradition says Leviathan and Behemoth are kept for the end of days. 1 Enoch 60:7–9 places the female Leviathan in the sea and the male Behemoth in a desert east of Eden; 4 Ezra 6:49–52 says God kept both from the fifth day of creation as food for whom he wills; 2 Baruch 29:4 says they will be food for those who are left in the days of the Messiah. The Talmud (Bava Batra 74b–75a) adds that God killed the female Leviathan and salted her for the righteous, that Gabriel will hunt the male, and that the righteous will feast on it and sit in booths made of its skin, reading Job 41:6–7. The prayer said on leaving the sukkah asks to be worthy to sit in the sukkah of Leviathan's skin.

"Will you haul Leviathan up on a fishhook?" (Job 41:1). Gregory the Great answered: Christ did. In his Moralia (book 33), the devil swallowed the bait of Christ's human flesh and was caught on the hook of his divinity; Gregory of Nyssa had used the same image (Catechetical Oration 24). Medieval art and preaching made this "fishhook" picture of the atonement popular. Many Protestants, starting with Calvin's sermons on Job, preferred to read a real animal and drew from it God's power over all creatures.

common: Leviathan in Job 41 is usually identified with the crocodile, or with the mythic sea monster, or with both at once.
uncommon: Some young-earth creationists read Leviathan as a surviving marine reptile or dinosaur.

claude.title: The monster with no fight
claude.body: In every other biblical use of the image, God fights the sea monster or will fight it (Psalm 74:13–14; Isaiah 27:1; Isaiah 51:9; Revelation 20:2), or plays with it (Psalm 104:26). In Job 41 alone there is no battle, only description and admiration. My reading is that this is the book's answer to Job's fear in Job 7:12: the chaos Job felt was loose against him is real, but it is a creature on God's leash, and God is not anxious about it. Habel and Newsom make related points.
claude.refs: Job 41:1–34; Job 7:12; Psalm 74:13–14; Psalm 104:26; Isaiah 27:1; Revelation 20:2

sections.b: God tells Job, "Look, please, at Behemoth, which I made as well as you. Like cattle, it feeds on grass" (Job 40:15). Its strength is in its hips and belly, its tail stiff like a cedar, its bones like bronze pipes (Job 40:16–18). It is "the first of the ways of God" (Job 40:19), the words Wisdom uses of herself in Proverbs 8:22. It lies among thorny lotus bushes and reeds, and a flood does not alarm it (Job 40:21–23). No one can catch it (Job 40:24).

The name is the plural of behemah, "beast", used for one creature: "the Beast". Hippopotamus: Bochart (1663) and most modern scholars, because of the grass, the reeds, the lotus and the river. Elephant: Aquinas, Calvin and many older writers. Mythic monster: Pope and John Day connect it with a bull-like monster killed by the goddess Anat at Ugarit, and later Jewish writings make it the land partner of Leviathan. Both: Othmar Keel shows that in Egypt the hippopotamus hunted by the king or by Horus stood for chaos, so a real animal could carry mythic meaning. Dinosaur: young-earth creationists such as Henry Morris read the cedar-like tail (Job 40:17) as a sauropod's; most scholars take the line as a euphemism or as poetic exaggeration.

sections.h: Behemoth in Jewish and Christian tradition
sections.b: 1 Enoch 60:7–9 says Behemoth is male, living in a desert called Dendayn east of Eden, and Leviathan female, in the sea; 4 Ezra 6:49–52 gives Behemoth the dry land with a thousand mountains; 2 Baruch 29:4 keeps both as food for the days of the Messiah. The rabbis linked Behemoth with the beasts "on a thousand hills" of Psalm 50:10 and with the feast of the righteous (Bava Batra 74b; Leviticus Rabbah 13:3). Gregory the Great read Behemoth as the devil, made "the first of the ways of God" as the greatest of angels before his fall.

common: Most modern scholars identify Behemoth with the hippopotamus, often with mythic overtones.
uncommon: Some identify Behemoth with a dinosaur, a view almost all biblical scholars reject.

sections.b: God answers Job with creation: "Where were you when I founded the earth?" (Job 38:4). The earth is a building with measured bases and a corner stone, set while "the stars of morning sang as one" (Job 38:7). The sea is a newborn God swaddles in cloud and gives a limit (Job 38:8–11). Snow and hail have storerooms; rain falls "on a desert where no person lives" (Job 38:26). Then come the animals, wild and mostly beyond human use, fed and freed by God (Job 38:39–39:30), and finally Behemoth and Leviathan (Job 40:15–41:34). The speeches teach that creation is far larger than human concerns, ordered but not tame, and wholly God's.

In Job the sea is not a defeated enemy but a baby: it bursts from the womb, and God dresses it in clouds and wraps it in deep darkness, then sets doors and a bolt: "Up to here you may come, but not one step more. Here a stop is set for your proud waves" (Job 38:11). Leviathan, its great creature, "brings the deep to a boil, like a cooking pot" (Job 41:31). The picture reworks the old myth of a storm god fighting the sea (compare Job 7:12; 26:12) into a picture of care and control.

sections.b: God asks, "Who has put wisdom in what lies hidden?" (Job 38:36) and "Who is wise enough to number the clouds?" (Job 38:37). The ostrich has none: "God has let wisdom slip from its mind" (Job 39:17). Behemoth is "the first of the ways of God" (Job 40:19), the phrase used of Wisdom in Proverbs 8:22. Job's answer is to admit that he spoke "without understanding, about wonders beyond me" (Job 42:3). The speeches confirm the poem of chapter 28: true wisdom is God's, and for humans it begins in awe.

Job's friends held that God always repays: the righteous prosper and the wicked suffer, so Job must have sinned. At the end the LORD tells Eliphaz, "I am furious with you and with your two friends. You did not say what is right about me, the way my servant Job did" (Job 42:7). The book thus denies that suffering always proves guilt. Yet it ends with Job's goods doubled (Job 42:10–12), so it does not deny that God blesses. Readers differ on whether the ending restores the rule of reward or simply shows God's free generosity after the rule has been broken.

common: The book of Job is widely read as a protest against the idea that all suffering is punishment.
uncommon: Some read the restored fortunes in Job 42 as a reaffirmation of reward and punishment, delayed but real.

sections.b: Job ends: "That is why I take back what I said, and I change my mind about dust and ashes" (Job 42:6). This site's Plain follows the retraction reading: the verb em'as "I reject" has no object, and "what I said" is supplied from Job 42:3; nicham 'al is the set phrase "change one's mind about" (Exodus 32:14). The traditional reading is repentance: "I despise myself and repent in dust and ashes" (KJV), supported by Job 7:16 and 9:21, where the same verb stands alone for Job's rejecting his own life, by Jeremiah 8:6, where nicham 'al means "repent of", by the Vulgate's "I rebuke myself and do penance", and by the Qumran Targum's "I shall become dust and ashes". Others read comfort (Clines: "I accept consolation for my dust and ashes"; Greenstein: "I take pity on dust and ashes") or rejection of God (Curtis). Whatever Job turns from, it is not the sins the friends alleged: God says Job spoke rightly (Job 42:7).
sections.refs: Job 42:1–7; Job 7:16; Job 9:21; Jeremiah 8:6; Exodus 32:14; Genesis 18:27

sections.b: The friends who said God would not hear Job must now ask Job to pray for them: "Job my servant will pray for you. I will accept him" (Job 42:8). Like Abraham praying for Abimelech (Genesis 20:7, 17) and Moses for Israel (Exodus 32:11–14), the righteous sufferer becomes the go-between. The restoration comes "when Job prayed for his friends" (Job 42:10). Ezekiel 14:14 names Job, with Noah and Daniel, among the great righteous men whose goodness counts before God.

sections.h: "Now my own eye has seen you" (Job 42:5)
sections.b: The LORD answers Job "from the windstorm" (Job 38:1; 40:6), the setting of Sinai (Exodus 19:16). Job says, "Before, I had only heard about you, but now my own eye has seen you" (Job 42:5). He sees no form; the seeing is the encounter itself. Maimonides read it as the move from tradition to true knowledge; many Christians read it as the heart of the book, where meeting God answers what argument could not.

sections.h: The sons of God at creation (Job 38:7)
sections.b: When God founded the earth "the stars of morning sang as one, and all the sons of God raised a shout" (Job 38:7). The heavenly beings who gather before God in Job 1:6 and 2:1 are here witnesses of creation, older than the earth. The Greek translation has "all my angels".

After his restoration Job has three daughters, Jemimah, Keziah and Keren-happuch, and "Their father gave them property to inherit side by side with their brothers" (Job 42:15). In Israel's law a daughter inherited only if there was no son (Numbers 27:8). Job, a man of Uz, goes beyond that. The Testament of Job (chapters 46–50) makes the daughters' inheritance heavenly sashes that let them speak the language of angels.

sections.h: Job as Jobab, king of Edom (Greek Job 42:17)
sections.b: The Greek ending of Job says that Job lived in Ausitis "on the borders of Idumea and Arabia", that his name before was Jobab, and that he was the second king of Edom after Balak son of Beor, "fifth from Abraham" through Esau. This comes from reading Genesis 36:33, "Jobab son of Zerah, from Bozrah, reigned in his place", as Job. The Testament of Job and the Jewish writer Aristeas also call Job Jobab. Eliphaz the Temanite is an Edomite name too (Genesis 36:11).

sections.h: The Accuser's silence at the end (Job 38–42)
sections.b: The Accuser who set the test in motion (Job 1:6–12; 2:1–7) never appears again. God does not mention him in the speeches from the storm, and the narrator says the family comforted Job "for all the harm the LORD had brought on him" (Job 42:11). Readers take the silence differently: the Accuser's role ended when Job did not curse God; the book refuses to let God's responsibility be passed to a lesser being; or the prose frame and the poem simply have different concerns. Christian readers who see Satan in Leviathan (Gregory the Great) find him in Job 41 in another form.

Job's last words confess that he spoke of "wonders beyond me" and that his hearing of God has become seeing (Job 42:3, 5). God then declares that the friends "did not say what is right about me, the way my servant Job did" (Job 42:7), and has Job pray for them. The LORD turns Job's fortunes around and doubles his flocks and herds (Job 42:10–12). He has seven sons and three daughters, the daughters named and given an inheritance, and he dies "old and satisfied with days" (Job 42:17), like Isaac (Genesis 35:29).
